faqs.question: What is the minimum a case study must contain?
faqs.answer: The constraint in the client's words, the decision you made, and a frame where that decision is visible. Then say how a similar buyer starts a project. Screenshots without those sentences are a gallery.

faqs.question: Should a case study include metrics?
faqs.answer: Only when the number is true and you are allowed to share it. A precise qualitative result, such as a reader finding a work or a customer finishing checkout, is stronger than an invented percentage. Do not borrow a result from a neighboring project.

faqs.question: Which project should you publish first?
faqs.answer: The one that matches the clients you want next, not the one with the most frames. One finished page beats five thin ones. If a favorite project is under embargo, write a different one rather than hiding the index behind a password.

markdown:
A creative studio case study page should show the constraint, the decision, and one decision visible in the work, for a client who has already seen fifty portfolios. Screenshots without a decision are decoration. End on how a similar buyer can start a project.

That is the whole assignment. A page that forgets any of the three parts becomes a gallery, and this buyer already has galleries bookmarked.

## Constraint, decision, result

Open the page with the constraint in the client's words. A heritage archive nobody could search. A store that had to move without a week of broken checkout. A brand whose team was inventing a new color every Friday. Time, audience, and what was not allowed to change. The constraint is why the decision was hard. Without it, the decision looks like taste.

Then name the decision in one or two sentences. What you cut. What you kept. What you refused to add. Thomas Bewick is easier to trust when the page says how an engraving archive became a place to read. Down the Cove is easier to trust when the page says what the migration kept so the shop still felt like the shop. Wabisabi is easier to trust when restraint is described as a choice, not as a filter.

Then show the result as something a similar buyer can recognize. A reader can find a work. A customer can finish checkout. A small team can publish a page without calling the studio. Metrics are optional. If you do not have a number you are allowed to share, do not invent one. A precise qualitative result beats a fake percentage.

Put those three parts before any film, any grid of angles, and any thank-you quote. The buyer who is scanning will take them and leave, or stay for the pictures because the pictures now have a job. [Research on generative search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) found that quotations, citations, and statistics made pages easier to surface, and that stuffing a page with repeated phrases made visibility worse, on the order of a ten percent drop. A proof page already has the raw material of a quotation: the decision, said once, in a sentence someone else could cite. Use that. Do not pad the page with synonyms of "creative."

## Screenshots are not the proof

A screenshot is evidence only after the sentence. Crop to the place the decision lives. The search field on the archive. The product grid after the cut. The type pair on a real article, not on a poster of the type pair. A frame of a whole homepage at laptop size, with no caption, asks the visitor to guess. Guesses are how trust leaks.

Sequence the images in the order of the argument. Before and after, if the before explains the constraint. A flow, if the decision was a path. A single still, if the decision was restraint and more frames would undo it. Three images that repeat the same point are a reel in disguise.

Do not open with a montage. Motion can show a transition that a still cannot, such as how a menu behaves or how a page settles. It should not be the first thing on the page, and it should not autoplay with sound. The client is reading for a choice. A film that starts before the sentence has already spent their patience.

Label what you did and what you did not do. Design. Build. Both. Brand only. If an engineer on the client side built the front end from your files, say that. Over-claiming is the fastest way to lose a buyer who has been in production. They can tell when a case study swallows the whole company.

## How long the page should be

Long enough to finish the decision. Short enough that you do not retell the kickoff. A useful shape is the constraint, the decision, two or three moments in the work, what you left out, and how a similar buyer starts. If you need twelve sections, you have started writing a process brochure.

Write in short paragraphs. Name the screens. Avoid a diary of every meeting. The buyer does not need your internal milestones. They need to see that the constraint survived contact with the real content.

A list helps when the decisions were a set:

- What you kept from the old site or the old brand.
- What you cut, and why.
- What the client can edit without you.
- What you would not repeat.

That list is more citable than a paragraph of atmosphere. It is also easier to skim on a phone, which is where many of these buyers will first open the project from a link you sent.

Quotes, if you use them, should say something the pictures cannot. A client describing the constraint in their words. Not "a pleasure to work with." If you do not have permission, skip the quote. The decision still stands.

## Which project to publish

Publish the project that matches the clients you want next, not the project with the most frames. A beautiful side piece will attract more side pieces. If you want stores, lead the index with the store. If you want editorial cultural work, lead with the archive. The proof page is a filter, and the filter should be intentional.

You need the client's permission, and you need assets you can show. If a favorite project is under a quiet period, write a different one. A locked case study with a password wall is a poor proof page for a cold buyer. Send passwords to people who already asked. Do not make the public page a locked door with a paragraph of adjectives in front of it.

One strong page beats five thin ones. A thin page is a row of images and a sentence about "collaborating closely." Delete it or finish it. An index of thin pages trains the buyer to expect decoration, which is the failure this whole site is trying to avoid.

Keep the writing in the studio's voice. Concrete nouns. The name of the page type. The name of the tool only when it changes the decision. Figma for the structure, a production front end in Next.js and TypeScript when you built it, Tailwind for the system, Motion where movement carried a point. Stack lists that do not connect to a decision are résumés, not proof.

## How the page should end

End on a similar buyer. One sentence that says who this project resembles, and the action to start a project. "If you are moving a store and need the catalog, the cart, and the brand to survive the move, start a project and send the current URL." That sentence is more useful than "want to create something amazing together."

Do not end on an award, a logo farm, or a related-posts widget that looks automatic. The last thing they read should be the path. Repeat the same action the homepage uses, so the site feels like one studio.

Point at one other proof page only if it shows a different decision. Two store migrations in a row is a specialty. A store migration and a brand system is a practice. Say which one they are opening and why. "A different constraint" is a better link label than "more work."

If you are building these pages and want a reference for how finished work is framed, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Read for the decision, not for the surface. Then ask whether your draft still makes sense with the images removed. If it does not, the sentences are not done.

## What not to claim

Do not invent results, timelines, or quotes. Do not imply a headcount, a prize, or a revenue figure. Do not say a project "transformed the brand" unless you can say what changed on the page. Do not publish a process that was not the process. Clients talk to each other. A polished fiction is a liability in a small market.

Do not stuff the page with the phrase you hope to rank for. Say what the project is, once, in the opening, and then use the names of the real objects. Archive. Checkout. Type. Grid. The ranking, if it comes, comes from a page a buyer can finish.

A short note on access belongs at the end if the work lives on. The client owns the repository and the content. Your proof page is a record, not a lock. Write it so it can stay true after launch, when the client edits a headline and the giant claim about every pixel would become false.

## A set of pages, not one masterpiece

Treat the index as a table of decisions. Each row is a constraint and a link. The visitor should be able to choose a relevant project without opening all of them. Filters are optional. Honest labels are not. "Site," "store," "brand," "product" are labels. "Selected," "featured," and "latest" are not, unless you also say selected for what.

When the index works, the next design problem is how people move among these pages without getting lost. [Navigation for a creative studio](/blog/navigation-for-a-creative-studio) is the piece to write next. The labels should match words the buyer already uses, and one path should start a project. A proof page that cannot be found from those labels is a PDF with a nicer template.
